Name: The Social Network of Roman Public Baths and the Street Rumors of the Subura
RagShortTexts: Roman public baths were the central places where the citizens of the whole city bathed, exercised, socialized and where politicians canvassed for votes
They consisted of a warm room, a hot room and a cold plunge pool, and bronze scrapers were used to remove olive oil and grime
The Subura slum, cramped and packed with taverns, was a breeding ground for wartime rumors and panic
BaseText: The public bath (Balneum) was the central nerve center of Roman urban society. Every afternoon, wealthy senators and poor plebeians alike paid a single copper coin to enter the baths. After taking off their togas, citizens rubbed themselves with olive oil and did wrestling and gymnastics, then passed in order through the warm room (Tepidarium) and the steaming hot room (Caldarium), and finally leapt into the icy cold pool (Frigidarium) to close their pores, while slaves scraped the oily grime and dead skin from their bodies with bronze strigils (Strigil). The baths echoed with debate, speeches and plots, and politicians, naked, courted the votes of the common people there. Right next to the bustling baths lay the Subura district, whose buildings rose six stories high yet were hastily built of planks and mud and easily caught fire or collapsed. Its small taverns were full of street rumors about surprise attacks by Hannibal's war elephants, soaring grain prices and corrupt senators, and it was the weathervane of the whole city's public mood.

Variants.Content: In the hot pool of the baths everyone is stark naked, and no one can tell a senator from a cobbler. Drink a bowl of hot barley beer, listen to the whispers in the Subura about the latest news from the front, and that is what it means to be alive!
The dark alleys of the Subura breed absurd rumors about the Carthaginians every day. If the tribunes do not bring order, those hysterical plebeian mobs will sooner or later set the Forum on fire.

I hold the bronze scraper and wipe down the backs of my arrogant Roman masters. They hold forth about the legions' slaughter overseas, never knowing that their empire has long been built on the spines of slaves.
